### 1.1 Precision genome editing

After the recognition that all of Earth’s biota was united in its usage of nucleic acids as

the mechanism for information transmission, and thereby propagation, the ensuing explosion in

scope of the life sciences has been centered around the manipulation of these molecules. Humans

have appreciated the utility of genome engineering since the onset of domesticated plants and

animals, breeding toward improved desirable traits such as hardiness or yield and unknowingly

altering the associated genomic sequences from their ancestral starting points in the process to a

radical degree. Selective breeding as a technique for genetic engineering however is inherently

clumsy, requiring the combination of whole sets of chromosomes each generation. Such large

transformations can quickly yield visibly discernible gains in desired phenotypes; however, this

often comes at the cost of undesirable traits riding along—many breeds of dogs are testament to

the capricious nature of this process1.

The advent of molecular cloning techniques, enabling programmable and precise changes

to the genetic content of amenable organisms such as bacteria2 and yeast3 at first, greatly

accelerated our ability to probe the underlying mechanisms by which the information encoded in

DNA enables all the complexities of life. Controlled genetic approaches to modifying proteins

and RNAs not only allowed scientists to isolate and decipher particular natural phenomena, but

also enabled the use of microorganisms for the production of useful compounds for industry4,5 or

medicine6. While cloning has become a routine process in laboratories all over the world, the

conditions involved, typically using harsh chemicals7, heat shock8, or electricity9 to permeabilize

cells, are not broadly applicable to multicellular organisms. And, as our increased understanding

of genetics led to the identification of the causative mutations for thousands of genetic diseases10,

particularly after the completion of the human genome project11, scientists and clinicians


<!-- Page 14 -->


3

increasingly appreciated the potential utility of genome editing technologies for treating these

human disorders.

In broad terms, conventional therapeutics tend to block a target molecular process by

competitive inhibition or allosteric modulation to elicit clinical benefit. Antibiotics inhibit

pathways vital for bacterial survival such as cell wall biosynthesis12, ACE inhibitors block the

activity of angiotensin-converting enzyme13 and statins lower cholesterol by inhibiting HMG-

CoA reductase14 among other potential notable examples. For most genetic diseases though, such

as Duchenne muscular dystrophy15 or spinal muscular atrophy16, pathology stems from a lack of

functional protein—in which case there is nothing to inhibit. Examples of drugs that can rescue

activity of dysfunctional proteins do exist, most notably Trikafta® for cystic fibrosis17, but these

success stories are unfortunately not generalizable. On the other hand, the existence of humans

who, not having the relevant pathological mutation, do not suffer from a particular genetic

disease, intrinsically suggests that reversing such mutations via genome editing can provide

therapeutic benefit. The question is whether this can be done effectively, safely, and early enough

in the course of the disease.

To be an effective therapeutic agent, genome editors must be highly precise given the

permanence of their effects. Undesired editing, beyond potentially introducing inactivating

mutations into healthy alleles of a specific affected cell, could cause systemic disease in the form

of mutagenesis-induced autoimmunity18 or cancer19. Given that the genome is composed of only

four different bases, achieving sufficient specificity therefore requires targeting a long enough

contiguous sequence of DNA such that only the desired locus in the genome is edited, with

perhaps the addition of similar sequences that can be characterized as benign sites for off-target

editing. Proteins, including meganucleases20, zinc fingers21, and transcription activator-like


<!-- Page 15 -->


4

effector nucleases (TALENs)22, have therefore predominated as a modality for the specific

recognition and manipulation of DNA given the number of molecular interactions required.

Undoubtably however, the most influential and broadly utilized family of proteins for

genome editing are the CRISPR-associated (Cas) proteins23, particularly Cas9 from

Streptococcus pyogenes (SpCas9)24. In large part this is due to the ease with which Cas proteins

can be programmed to recognize specific DNA sequences: altering the spacer sequence of the

guide RNA molecule bound by a Cas protein is sufficient to target the corresponding protospacer

sequence in the genome so long as it is adjacent to a minimal protospacer-adjacent motif (PAM)

sequence, such as NGG for SpCas925. While guide RNAs are endogenously a two-part system

comprised of a spacer-containing CRISPR RNA (crRNA) hybridized with a trans-activating

crRNA (tracrRNA) that is bound by the Cas protein, as part of genome editing technologies these

elements are typically fused into a single guide RNA (sgRNA) for efficiency and ease of use24.

The first uses of SpCas9 for mammalian genome editing relied on its native ability to

induce double-strand breaks (DSBs) in the target DNA protospacer sequence26,27. Clinically, this

can be used to knock out dominant pathogenic alleles in heterozygous individuals when the

remaining healthy allele is haplosufficient28, disrupt transcription factor binding sites as a

compensatory strategy29, convert pathogenic alleles to healthy variants when favored by

microhomology-mediated repair30, engineer cell therapies31, and introduce specified DNA donor

sequences via endogenous mammalian homology-directed repair (HDR) pathways25. This last

application is the most versatile, but HDR is inefficient in most therapeutically relevant types of

cells32 and is in competition with non-homologous end joining (NHEJ)33. In addition, the

superior kinetics of the NHEJ pathway over HDR means that the signature of NHEJ repair,

stochastic small insertions or deletions (indels), are usually in excess of the desired incorporation


<!-- Page 16 -->


5

of the donor sequence34. DSBs themselves are associated with a multitude of deleterious

consequences, including translocations35, p53 activation36, large deletions37, and

chromothrypsis38.

The inability to control the outcomes of SpCas9 nuclease activity have greatly hindered

its adoption in the clinic for genome editing. However, the ability of SpCas9 to target specified

DNA sequences with precision has proven instrumental in enabling the development of two key

next-generation precision genome editing technologies: base editing and prime editing39. In each,

the problems presented by DSB formation are sidestepped via the introduction of mutations into

the nuclease domains of SpCas9 that convert it to a DNA nickase24; these mutations are D10A

within the RuvC domain for base editors40 and H840A within the HNH domain for prime

editors41. Moreover, genome editing is instead carried out via the fusion of novel enzymatic

domains to the SpCas9 nickase that act upon the single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) R-loop

generated upon protospacer recognition. While base and prime editors using a variety of

orthologues of SpCas9 have been developed that vary in PAM preference, size, and activity42-46,

SpCas9-based variants remain the closest to clinical use and are the primary focus of this

introduction.

Base editors are comprised of a cytosine40 or adenine47 deaminase fused to a Cas9

protein. Deamination of cytosine directly produces uracil, which is equivalent in base-pairing

properties to thymine, whereas adenine deamination generates inosine, mimicking guanine. In

both cases, cellular DNA repair processes eventually mediate replacement of the intermediate

uracil or inosine product with thymine or guanine for successful editing events, effecting C•G-to-

T•A or A•T-to-G•C transition mutations respectively. Genome editing specificity is ensured by


<!-- Page 17 -->


6

the exquisite selectivity of the deaminases for ssDNA, meaning that editing activity is dependent

on the formation of an R-loop, i.e., on successful protospacer binding by SpCas9.

Off-target mutagenesis of bystander bases within the target protospacer, bases exposed by

off-target binding by SpCas948, or bases in ssDNA made available by unrelated processes such as

within replication bubbles49, have been characterized for base editors. However, deamination is

theoretically a far less perturbative event, not sharing any of the previously described cellular

consequences resulting from DSB formation. Adenine base editors (ABEs) are particularly

specific50, likely due to the deoxyadenosine deaminase domain having undergone laboratory

evolution from an RNA-specific adenine deaminase and therefore having little native affinity for

ssDNA47. While cytosine base editors (CBEs) exhibit higher rates of off-target editing50, in part

due to the incorporation of a uracil glycosylase inhibitor domain in the most efficient iterations40,

engineering efforts have produced variants with greatly improved ratios of on-target to off-target

editing for sensitive applications49.

The functional scope of base editing for therapeutics is limited to what can be

accomplished via any of the four transition mutations: C•G-to-T•A or A•T-to-G•C directly and

G•C-to-A•T or T•A-to-C•G by editing the opposite strand. Base editors capable of mediating

transversion mutations such as C•G-to-G•C have been described51-55, but in all cases require the

formation of abasic sites that result in impure product formation, precluding clinical use.

However, 30% of known human pathogenic genetic variants are single-nucleotide

polymorphisms (SNPs) that can be reversed in principle with base editors41. In addition,

transition mutations can be used to treat diseases without directly reversing causative mutations,

such as by installing alternative non-pathogenic variants56, altering transcript splicing57 or


<!-- Page 18 -->


7

multiplexed engineering of cell therapies58, further expanding the scope of therapeutic base

editing applications.

Prime editing bears no such restrictions with respect to the types of genomic edits it can

produce. This functional versatility is made possible by the sequence-dependent mechanism of

action employed by prime editors, which consist of a Cas9 protein fused with a reverse

transcriptase (RT) and bound to a prime editing guide RNA (pegRNA)59. After nicking of the

protospacer-containing DNA strand by H840A SpCas9, the liberated strand is able to hybridize

with the 3′ extension of the pegRNA—this key feature, containing a reverse transcriptase

template (RTT) sequence that programs the RT and a primer binding site (PBS) sequence that is

complementary to the protospacer, is what differentiates pegRNAs from sgRNAs. Formation of

an RNA:DNA duplex between the PBS and the nicked protospacer primes the reverse

transcription of the RTT, allowing any encoded edit within to be transferred into the newly

synthesized 3′ DNA flap. This edit can then be permanently incorporated into the genome

following successful resolution of the competing 5′ unedited flap60 and other cellular DNA repair

pathways such as mismatch repair45.

All point mutations as well as insertions and deletions, including combinations thereof,

are possible edits using prime editing. Smaller insertions and deletions tend to be more efficient,

both as a function of RT processivity and strand invasion by the edited flap in order to

rehybridize with the genome61, but twin prime editing approaches62 and other strategies

involving two complementary RT products63-66 have extended the scale of efficient edits to the

order of hundreds of bases. Furthermore, the mechanism of prime editing requires three distinct

sequence-dependent hybridization events—protospacer recognition, PBS binding, and finally RT

product integration—whereas Cas9 nucleases and base editors require only the first event in this


<!-- Page 19 -->


8

sequence before editing can commence. These additional checks for proper localization within

the genome grant prime editing the most precision out of any genome editing technology

developed so far. Indeed, several studies performing whole genome off-target analysis67-69 have

shown off-target editing by prime editors to be minimal if detectable at all. Altogether, the

flexibility of prime editing, theoretically enabling reversal of 89% of known human pathogenic

variants41, coupled with its exquisite selectivity, lends credence to it having significant and broad

clinical potential if key remaining challenges can be addressed.

While prime editing does not require the formation of a DSB, including an sgRNA that

directs the editor to nick the unedited DNA strand is an effective method for generally improving

editing efficiency41. This helps direct DNA repair machinery to use the edited strand as a

template for resolving the edit-induced mismatch, as nicks are commonly recognized by cells as

a sign of DNA damage70. The two nicks are spatially separated but can still lead to indels, albeit

to a much lesser degree than nucleases, if perturbed by cellular events such as entering a

replication fork or chew-back by exonucleases during DNA repair71. Despite incurring the

drawbacks of DSB formation, secondary nicking with sgRNAs is often necessary to achieve

sufficient editing efficiency—the elaborate mechanism of prime editing, while precise, is

generally less efficient than base editing for achieving the same edit, having many more possible

points of failure. In certain applications wherein a suitable PAM is located between the pegRNA-

targeted protospacer and the edit, such that the spacer of the sgRNA can be chosen to be

complementary to the RT product after Cas9 binds the PAM, temporal separation of the two

nicks can achieved. This greatly reduces indel formation while preserving the benefits of nicking

the unedited strand but cannot be utilized in all cases. Less mitigable is the large size of the

prime editor protein: the coding sequence of the original, SpCas9 fused to the RT from Moloney


<!-- Page 20 -->


9

murine leukemia virus, is approximately 6400 base pairs. This presents a substantial challenge

for in vivo delivery of prime editors, which many unrealized clinical genome editing applications

require, because adeno-associated viruses cannot package such a sizeable transgene.

### 1.2 Adeno-associated viral vectors for in vivo delivery of genome editors

Adeno-associated viruses (AAVs) are small 26-nm icosahedral viruses of the

Parvoviridae family72. As implied by their name, these viruses require co-infection by adenovirus

to complete their life cycle and as a result were originally isolated as a contaminant in

preparations of adenovirus73. From these serendipitous origins, replication-incompetent AAV

vectors have become the premiere method of in vivo gene delivery as evidenced by FDA

approvals of AAV therapies for retinal dystrophy74, spinal muscular atrophy75, hemophilia B76,

Duchenne muscular dystrophy77 and hemophilia A78. The widespread success of AAV compared

to competing novel methods of transgene delivery is in large part due to its favorable safety

profile. Unlike retroviruses, AAVs are not known to cause disease in humans and rarely integrate

into the genome except for an established safe-harbor locus called AAVS179. Furthermore, AAVs

are considered less immunogenic compared to other viral delivery strategies, in part due to poor

transduction of antigen-presenting cells80 but also due to not needing to include any viral coding

sequences for successful transgene encapsulation72.

The native genomic components encoded within AAV are quite minimal, consisting only

of two open reading frames, rep and cap, that respectively encode Rep78, Rep68, Rep52 and

Rep40 or VP1, VP2 and VP3 via alternative start codons and splicing. This simplicity allows in

vitro production of AAV vectors through transient expression of the assorted helper and capsid

proteins81. The only native elements required for successful transgene incorporation into AAV

particles are the inverted terminal repeats (ITRs). These structured non-coding sequences serve


<!-- Page 21 -->


10

as a packaging signal and primer for second-strand synthesis post-transduction to convert the

single-stranded AAV genome into a double-stranded episome capable of expressing the cargo

cassette82.

Aside from safety considerations, AAVs are also able to efficiently transduce a variety of

distinct tissue and cell types. The tropism of an AAV particle is governed by the specific cell

surface receptor affinities intrinsic to the capsid serotype being used. By swapping the capsid

serotype used during vector production, tissue tropism, activity and immunogenicity can easily

be tailored to a given application83. This last point in particular, given the varying prevalence of

pre-existing neutralizing antibodies specific to different AAV serotypes84 within human

populations, is a valuable characteristic for extending the benefits of AAV therapies to the largest

possible number of patients. Beyond the native tissue tropisms possessed by natural AAV

serotypes, engineering and directed-evolution efforts have yielded novel capsid sequences with

improved or novel transduction characteristics, such as a preference for muscle tissues85 or the

ability to cross the blood brain barrier86.

The safety and flexibility with which AAVs can deliver transgene cargos in vivo has

made them an attractive candidate for mediating in vivo genome editing. However, an obstacle

of particular note has been the limited cargo capacity of AAV; transgene packaging efficiency

drops exponentially past the consensus limit of roughly 4.7 kb87. The additional molecular

functionality necessary for precision genome editing imparts large size requirements in addition

to the considerable size of SpCas9, the coding sequence of which is 4.1 kb already. SpCas9-

based base editors and prime editors reach 5.4 and 6.4 kb respectively, well beyond the AAV

packaging limit even before considering need for promoters, guide RNAs, and other regulatory

sequences. To address this limitation, researchers have developed strategies to split genome


<!-- Page 22 -->


11

editor sequences between two viruses that then reconstitute full-length editors upon co-

transduction88-91, in addition to the use of smaller Cas9 orthologues43 and trimming of protein

domains61,92. In particular, trans-splicing inteins such as from Nostoc punctiforme93 have

successfully been used to demonstrate efficient base editing and prime editing in vivo94,95.

### 1.3 Cancer immunology

Since the intimate relationship between the immune system and cancer was demonstrated

by the finding that immunocompromised mice developed tumors more often and more rapidly

than wild-type animals96, the modern field of immuno-oncology has created a paradigm shift in

our understanding and treatment of cancer. In particular, with cancer now recognized as a

continuously evolving and heterogeneous pathology, modulating the immune system has

emerged as an attractive avenue for developing new therapeutics because it is able to respond

and adapt in kind. Current immunotherapies such as immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs), cancer

vaccines, and chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells are available for a wide array of cancers

including melanoma, renal cell carcinoma, and acute lymphoblastic leukemia97-99.

However, as with any developing technology, despite the exciting advances that have

been made there are still important hurdles to be overcome. For ICIs, widely adopted for their

ability to induce astonishingly deep and lasting tumor regressions by blocking T cell exhaustion

pathways like the interaction between programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1) and its ligand

programmed cell death ligand 1 (PD-L1)100, a majority of cancer patients still do not respond to

treatment101. Though mechanisms of resistance remain a very active area of research, a

biomarker that has emerged as a predictor of ICI efficacy is the tumor mutation burden (TMB); a

higher rate of non-synonymous mutations is significantly correlated with a higher response rate

to PD-1/PD-L1 inhibition102. This finding suggests that some low-mutation-burden cancers


<!-- Page 23 -->


12

manage to evade detection by the immune system, and thereby do not respond to PD-1/PD-L1

inhibition, by presenting fewer mutated peptide sequences that can be used to distinguish

between healthy and cancerous cells.

There are a variety of mechanisms understood to enable recognition and destruction of

cancer cells by the immune system, but a primary effector is CD8+ cytotoxic T lymphocyte

(CTL) recognition of peptides presented on major histocompatibility complex class I (MHC-I)

molecules103. Such peptides are usually 8–11 residues long and are derived from the proteasomal

degradation of cytosolic proteins produced by the presenting cell104. MHC-I molecules originally

evolved as a strategy to identify cells infected by intracellular pathogens; their presence is

revealed to the immune system by the presentation of peptides originating from the proteins of

the pathogen. Targeting of healthy cells by immune system effectors is avoided by a strong

tolerization process to host proteins during effector cell development105,106. However, cancer

cells inherently exhibit some degree of genetic instability in order to develop a malignant

phenotype, and this trait leads to the accrual of tumor-specific mutations107. When non-

synonymous, such mutations can produce neoepitopes: novel peptide sequences that T cells can

target in order to specifically eliminate cancer cells108.

Much of the discussion surrounding the efficacy of current immunotherapies has been

focused on the oncolytic activities of CTLs mediated by recognition of neoepitopes presented on

MHC-I. Increasingly however, more recent studies are beginning to demonstrate the importance

of other lineages of the immune system in the antitumor response. CD4+ T cells, which lack

direct lytic abilities but direct other elements of the adaptive immune system via cytokine

signaling, were shown to be necessary for tumor rejection and generation of tumor-specific CTLs

in a murine sarcoma model that lacked MHC class II (MHC-II) expression109. MHC-II molecules


<!-- Page 24 -->


13

are the critical binding partner for CD4+ T cell activation and typically present peptides 13–25

residues in length104. As opposed to MHC-I, MHC-II expression is typically restricted to

professional antigen-presenting cells (APCs) such as B cells and dendritic cells (DCs). In

keeping with the role of these cells in detecting extracellular pathogens, the peptides displayed

by MHC-II are generated from the proteolytic cleavage of endocytosed proteins110. Therefore,

the finding that expression of an MHC-II epitope is necessary for rejection of an MHC-II-/- tumor

suggests that APCs are mediating presentation to and activation of CD4+ T cells. This

mechanism would enable CD4+ T cells to react to all types of tumors rather than just those

expressing MHC-II, indicating that they may have a much more general and important role in the

antitumor response than previously appreciated.

In a model where CD4+ T cell activation is critical for generating an antitumor response,

it follows that subsequent B cell activation may also be an important factor. Among the various

immune responses that CD4+ T cells can promote in response to MHC-II recognition, activating

naïve B cells as well as directing isotype switching of the resulting antibodies are commonly

performed functions111. Studies analyzing patient tumor samples before and after ICI treatment

have reported significant enrichment of B cell RNA signatures in the tumors of patients who

responded positively to ICI112-114. While the mechanisms by which B cells contribute to the

antitumor response are not yet fully understood, a markedly higher proportion of memory B cells

were detected in tumors that respond to ICI whereas naïve B cells predominated in the tumors of

non-responders112. Memory B cells have undergone selection to produce high-affinity antibodies

in response to recognition of an antigen115; their presence in responding tumors implies that

tumor-specific antigen recognition by B cells, which would drive memory B cell localization to

the tumor, contributes to successful tumor rejection. In contrast, tumors have previously been


<!-- Page 25 -->


14

shown to be able to induce an immunosuppressive phenotype in naïve B cells as an escape

strategy116,117. Such a process could be the reason for the observed increased proportion of naïve

B cells in unresponsive tumors.

Taken together, current research in immuno-oncology now indicates the necessity of

multiple arms of the adaptive immune system—CD8+ T cells, CD4+ T cells and B cells in

particular—to be engaged in order to form a durable antitumor response. However, a key

commonality between these lineages is that activation ultimately hinges on antigen recognition.

And yet, most non-synonymous mutations do not generate immunogenic epitopes. An analysis of

the MC38 cancer cell line, a widely used syngeneic mouse tumor model, detected 1290 amino

acid changes via exome sequencing but found only seven of those mutations presented on MHC-

I using mass spectrometry118. A number of factors exist which might rule out a mutation from

being efficiently presented on MHC-I. Aside from needing to occur in an expressed transcript

region, any mutations must compete for presentation with all the other peptides generated by the

proteasome, the vast majority of which will be wild-type sequences. Furthermore, in order for a

peptide to be bound tightly by MHC-I, it must possess the correct amino acids at anchor residue

positions within the peptide119. Finally, CD8+ T cell recognition of a presented peptide is

mediated by binding MHC-I via the T cell receptor (TCR), which generally interacts with

residues 3–7 within the peptide; the differentiating amino acid change must occur within this

region to elicit a strong response118. These limitations on epitope presentation, which also exist

for MHC-II104, provide a mechanism for the poor immunogenicity of cancers with low TMB.

Indeed, an analysis of the low-immunogenicity TRAMP-C1 mouse tumor cell line observed 949

non-synonymous mutations, of which 67 were expressed, but 0 were detected on MHC-I via

mass spectrometry118. This demonstration that cells can develop a malignant phenotype without


<!-- Page 26 -->


15

detectable presentation of neoepitopes is supportive of the hypothesis that possessing low TMB

is an effective strategy for immune evasion.

### 2.1 Introduction

CLN2 Batten disease, also known as late-infantile neuronal ceroid lipofuscincosis, is a

rare autosomal recessive disorder resulting from mutations in the TPP1 gene120. Despite a high

level of genetic heterogeneity, two predominant mutations account for over 50% of CLN2

disease diagnoses: an exonic c.622C>T transition resulting in the nonsense mutation p.R208X,

and an intronic mutation c.509-1G>C causing altered splicing, both of which result in

dysfunction of the soluble lysosomal protein tripeptidyl peptidase 1 (TPP1) and subsequent loss

of TPP1 enzyme activity121. CLN2 disease generally manifests between 2–4 years of age and has

a highly predictable disease progression. Symptoms include progressive vison loss, epileptic

seizures, ataxia, cognitive decline, and premature death by the second decade of life122.

Pathologically, TPP1 dysfunction results in lysosomal accumulation of storage material,

microglial and astrocyte activation, and severe neuronal loss.

Despite years of research, no curative treatment for CLN2 disease exists. An enzyme

replacement therapy, Brineura® (cerliponase alfa), remains the only FDA approved treatment

available to patients. Although cerliponase alfa has proven efficacious in certain aspects of

disease, its high cost, invasive administration procedure consisting of repeated dosing via an

intraventricular port, and inability to halt disease progression necessitate improved treatment

options123. Unlike enzyme replacement, gene editing approaches offer the potential for a curative

therapy by correcting underlying disease-causing mutations without the need for repeated dosing.

Previously a CLN2 mouse model, Cln2R207X-/-, was reported with homozygosity for Tpp1

R207X124. The coding sequence (CDS) of murine Tpp1 is one codon shorter than human TPP1

prior to the pathogenic mutation, hence the model corresponds with the most common human

CLN2 mutation TPP1 R208X. This model faithfully recapitulates both the pathology and the


<!-- Page 29 -->


18

motor deficits of CLN2, with accumulating disease burden leading to premature death beginning

roughly at 12 weeks of age. By closely emulating the human pathogenic locus, the Cln2R207X-/-

mouse enables more rigorous assessment of precision gene editing strategies on a target sequence

with greater clinical relevance for CLN2.

To gain deeper insights into CLN2 disease and explore improved therapeutic avenues, we

assessed the potential of adenine base editors (ABEs) to treat disease in Cln2R207X -/- mice124.

ABEs are a precision genome editing technology capable of catalyzing A•T-to-G•C transition

mutations within a 4–6 nucleotide (nt) editing window without requiring double-strand breaks in

target DNA sequences47,125. This enables reversion of the premature TGA stop codon back to a

healthy CGA codon encoding arginine by base editing TCA to TCG in the complementary

strand. Restoration of TPP1 function by genomic correction would potentially arrest disease

progression permanently, as TPP1 is secreted and taken up by neighboring cells, enabling

unedited cell rescue126,127. Given the reports that transgenes expressed from adeno associated

viruses (AAVs) are subject to degrees of silencing over time for multiple animal models, tissues

and promoters128-130, a one-time adenine base editing strategy for CLN2 could be a useful

alternative to other therapies such as enzyme replacement or gene therapy.

Here we report the development and characterization of an ABE strategy using SpCas9–

ABE7.10 for the correction of Tpp1 p.R207X. Eleven weeks after a single P1

intracerebroventricular (ICV) injection, Cln2R207X-/- mice treated with SpCas9–ABE7.10 showed

reversion of the nonsense mutation in the CNS up to 45% in the cortex. These levels of editing

were associated with significant reductions in markers of CLN2 pathology such as ATP synthase

subunit C accumulation, microgliosis, and astrocytosis131,132. Our results indicate that adenine

base editing has significant clinical potential as a single-dose therapy for CLN2 Batten disease.

### 2.2 Results

2.2.1 Editing strategy design

Tpp1 R207X can be corrected with adenine base editing using a variety of different

deaminase and Cas9 domains that confer different editing efficiencies, editing windows, and

required cargo sizes for in vivo delivery. Inspection of the target locus suggested that targeting

available protospacers for SpCas9 or SaCas9 would optimally position R207X for correction

within the editing window and minimize potential non-silent bystander editing (Figure 2.1a). We

therefore elected to test SpCas9 nickase fused to ABE7.1047, ABE8e125, and ABE8eV106W133

deaminases in preparation for an intein-split dual AAV strategy94, and SaCas9 nickase fused to

ABE8eV106W, which would fit within a single AAV43. To do so, we electroporated primary

mouse embryonic fibroblasts derived from Cln2R207X-/- mice with mRNAs encoding the specified

ABEs and the corresponding sgRNA. 48 hours post electroporation, we measured the most bulk

correction of R207X, up to 45.0 ± 5.0% (mean ± s.d.), using SpCas9–ABE8e in agreement with

previously reported activities125 (Figure 2.1b). Non-silent bystander editing was comparatively

minimal; using the SpCas9 protospacer as a reference, the next-most edited adenine aside from

A5 in R207X was A9 (up to 16.2 ± 5.1% with SpCas9–ABE8e). A•T-to-G•C conversion at this

position results in a silent CGT to CGC mutation in the coding strand, a feature that is conserved

in the human pathogenic allele (Figure 2.1a).

by ABE treatment revealed up to 7.7 ± 1.1% of R207X-corrected reads were accompanied by

non-silent bystander mutations (Figure 2.1c). Observing that up to 80% of the detected non-silent

### 2.3 Discussion

Here we describe and characterize an adenine base editor (ABE) strategy for the

correction of the most common pathogenic mutation found in patients with CLN2 Batten

disease: TPP1 p.R208X. When applied to Cln2R207X-/- mice bearing the equivalent mutation,

Tpp1 p.R207X, SpCas9–ABE7.10 treatment prevented progression of disease in the cortex and

hippocampus as measured by staining for CD68, glial fibrillary acidic protein, and ATP synthase

subunit C, maintaining each of these pathological markers at levels close or equivalent to WT

mice. These striking physiological effects were mediated by 26.5% correction of the mutation in

the cortex after discarding editing accompanied by bystander mutations (Figure 2.3d), with

presumably reduced correction in the hippocampus and thalamus corresponding with less

efficient transduction of these regions (Figure 2.3b). While highly promising, further studies to

demonstrate long-term survival benefit from editing and off-target analysis of the editing strategy

in human genomes must be performed prior to further clinical development.

The Y208H bystander mutation, which is conserved in the human sequence as Y209H

(Figure 2.1a), presents a potential obstacle to adenine base editing being an effective therapeutic

for CLN2. AAV vectors are currently the best modality for in vivo gene delivery to the CNS, but


<!-- Page 43 -->


32

the long-term expression of their cargo allows for the accumulation of less-efficient bystander

editing72. While this present study achieved substantial rescue using SpCas9–ABE7.10, the least

active of the tested editors (Figure 2.1b), use of deaminases with higher activity such as

ABE8eV106W would presumably mediate greater correction in regions that are transduced less

efficiently such as the thalamus. Their use, however, is precluded by probable increased

prevalence of the inactivating Y208H mutation offsetting any potential gains in therapeutic

efficacy. Technologies for in vivo editor delivery with limited expression, such as virus-like

particles134, should be further developed with aims toward improved CNS transduction in mind.

In addition, the human, but not mouse, sequence context of TPP1 p.R208X permits use of

SpCas9 protospacers that shift the pathogenic T•A base pair to position four or three due to

alternate codon usage for T201 and P202 (Figure 2.1a). Targeting these protospacers respectively

shifts the adenine responsible for Y209H to position one or outside the protospacer entirely,

which may reduce prevalence of this bystander mutation to acceptable levels even when using

more active deaminases.

In summary, this work demonstrates that adenine base editing has significant therapeutic

potential for the treatment of CLN2. Use of precision gene editing to correct the pathogenic

mutation can potentially lead to permanent arrest of disease progression through cross-correction

of neighboring cells despite likely eventual silencing of the transgene128. Given the recent

inability of AAV-delivered TPP1 gene therapy to slow disease progression more so than current

enzyme replacement therapy144, future studies should continue to investigate the viability of

adenine base editing as an alternative therapeutic strategy.

### 2.4 Methods

Animal Ethics Statement

Wild type (WT) and homozygous Cln2R207X-/- mice on C57BL/6j backgrounds were used

for all studies. All animals were housed and maintained under identical conditions at an

AAALAC accredited facility in accordance with Institutional Animals Care and Use Committee

(IACUC) protocol (Sanford Research, Sioux Falls, SD).

General methods

Plasmids were cloned with Gibson assembly and purified with Plasmid Plus Midiprep

kits (Qiagen). DNA amplification was performed by PCR using Phusion U Hotstart DNA

polymerase (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Primers were ordered from Integrated DNA

Technologies. Synthetic sgRNAs were ordered from Synthego with 2′-O-methyl modifications

in, and phosphorothioate bonds between, the first three and last three nucleotides.

General mammalian cell culture conditions

Unless otherwise specified, cells were cultured in media consisting of Dulbecco’s

Modified Eagle Medium (DMEM) with high glucose (Gibco), 4 mM L-glutamine, and 1 mM

sodium pyruvate supplemented with 10% (v/v) fetal bovine serum (FBS) (Gibco, qualified) and

1% Penicillin-Streptomycin (PS). Neuro2A (N2A) cells were purchased from the American Type

Culture Collection (ATCC). All cell lines were authenticated by the corresponding supplier and

routinely tested negative for mycoplasma contamination. Cells were passaged in 10-cm dishes

(Corning) and incubated at 37 °C with 5% CO2.


<!-- Page 45 -->


34

Mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEF) generation and culture

On embryonic day 15.5, a pregnant dam was euthanized via CO2 asphyxiation followed

by cervical dislocation. The uterus was exposed and embryos were removed by dissection with

scissors. The head and visceral organs were removed and discarded. The remaining tissue was

minced with a razor blade and incubated with 0.25% trypsin (Gibco) for 15 minutes at 37 °C.

Trypsin was inhibited by adding an equivalent volume of media. After passing the cell mixture

through a 70 µm nylon mesh filter, the cells were pelleted by centrifugation at 300g for 5

minutes and then resuspended in media before plating.

In vitro transcription of ABE mRNA

mRNA encoding ABEs was generated by in vitro transcription (IVT) as previously

described59. Briefly, mRNA transcription templates containing a 5′ untranslated region (UTR),

Kozak sequence, ABE ORF and 3′ UTR were generated by PCR using primers that install a T7

promoter and poly(A) tail at the 5′ and 3′ termini of the template respectively. IVT was

conducted using the HiScribe T7 High-Yield RNA kit (New England Biosciences) according to

the manufacturer’s protocols with full N1-methylpseudouridine (TriLink Biotechnologies)

substitution and co-transcriptionally capped with CleanCap AG (TriLink Biotechnologies).

Length and integrity of IVT products were verified using High Sensitivity RNA ScreenTape on

an Agilent TapeStation 4150.

ABE mRNA electroporation

WT or Tpp1 R207X-/- MEFs grown to 60–80% confluency were trypsinized and then

washed with 1× PBS (Gibco). In each cuvette, 2 × 105 cells were resuspended in 20 µL of

complete electroporation buffer with 1 µg of ABE mRNA and 50 pmol of sgRNA, and then

electroporated using a Lonza 4D-Nucleofector (program DS-150) and P2 primary cell kit


<!-- Page 46 -->


35

(Lonza). 80 µL of 37 °C media was then added to each cuvette before incubating the cells at

room temperature for 10 minutes. 1.6 × 105 cells were then plated in a T25 flask for enzyme

activity and 4 × 104 cells were plated per well in 48-well poly-D-lysine coated plates (Corning)

for sequencing. Cells were analyzed 2 days after electroporation for each assay.

High-throughput sequencing of genomic DNA samples

In vitro cultured cells were washed with 1× PBS and then lysed by the addition of 150 µL

of lysis buffer (10 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.0; 0.05% SDS; 25 µg/mL proteinase K (ThermoFisher

Scientific)). After incubating at 37 °C for 1 hour, lysates were inactivated by incubating at 80 °C

for 30 minutes and then used directly as template for PCR. Tissue samples were digested and the

genomic DNA extracted using the Agencourt DNAdvance kit (Beckman Coulter) per the

manufacturer’s protocol. Loci of interest were amplified and sequenced on an Illumina Miseq as

described previously134. After demultiplexing using Miseq Reporter software (Illumina), reads

were aligned to a reference sequence and quantified for editing using CRISPResso2 (145). Reads

were filtered for an average Phred quality score of 30 or higher prior to analysis.

Plasmid transfection

Neuro2As were plated at 1 × 105 cells/mL in 2 mL of media supplemented with 3% FBS

and 1% PS per well in a 6-well plate. The following day, cells were transfected using

Lipofectamine 3000 per the manufacturer’s protocol (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Briefly, 7.5 μL

of Lipofectamine 3000 was diluted with 125 μL Opti-MEM (Gibco) per well. Next, 2500 ng of

plasmid DNA was diluted to 125 μL with Opti-MEM and 5 μL P3000 per well. Finally, 125 μL

diluted Lipofectamine 3000 solution was combined with 125 μL of the diluted DNA solution per

well and incubated at room temperature for 10 minutes. Lastly, 150 μL of the complete


<!-- Page 47 -->


36

transfection solution was added to the media of the plated cells. After a 48 hour incubation, cells

were assessed for enzyme activity.

Enzyme activity

Cells were rinsed with ice-cold 1× PBS and scraped gently from each well. The samples

were centrifuged for 5 minutes at 4 °C at 200g and each resulting pellet was resuspended in 200

µL ice-cold lysis buffer (0.2% Triton X-100, 150 mM NaCl, 0.3% NP-40, 50 mM Tris-HCl pH

7.4, Protease and Phosphatase Inhibitor Cocktail, and 100 µM phenylmethanesulfonylfluoride)

and incubated on ice for 10 minutes. Samples were centrifuged for 5 minutes at 4 °C at 600g and

supernatants were transferred to fresh tubes. Following protein quantification, 10 µg of each

sample, as quantified by BCA assay, was added to a 96-well plate containing 40 µL TPP1

substrate and incubated for one hour in the dark at 37 °C. Subsequently, 200 µL TPP1 stop buffer

was added to each well. Finally, plates were analyzed using a BioTek Cytation 3 (Excite 380

nm/Emit 460 nm for TPP1).

Virus production

Recombinant AAV9 (rAAV) vectors were generated as previously described43,94 with

alterations described as follows. Briefly, HEK293T clone 17 (ATCC) cells were passaged in

DMEM with GlutaMAX (Gibco) supplemented with 10% FBS and passaged every 2–3 days to

avoid overconfluency in 15 cm dishes (CellTreat). Cells were split 1:3 one day prior to

transfection with 5.7 μg AAV genome, 11.4 μg pHelper (Clontech) and 22.8 μg AAV9 rep-cap

plasmid per plate using high molecular weight (MW) polyethylenimine (Polysciences). Media

was exchanged for 5% FBS DMEM with GlutaMAX 24 hours after transfection. After a further

72 hour incubation, cells were harvested with a rubber cell scraper (Corning) and pelleted by

centrifugation at 3,200g for 10 minutes. Pellets were then lysed by addition of 333 µL per plate


<!-- Page 48 -->


37

of high salt lysis buffer (40 mM Tris base, 500 mM NaCl, 2 mM MgCl2 and 100 U/mL salt

active nuclease (ArcticZymes, 70910–202)) and incubation at 37 °C for 1 hour. The media was

separately brought to 8% poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG) and 500 mM NaCl with a 40% PEG (8000

MW; Sigma Aldrich) 2.5 M NaCl 5× stock solution and then incubated at 4 °C for 2 hours before

being centrifuged for 30 minutes at 3,200g. The resulting pellets were then resuspended in 333

µL of high salt buffer per plate and combined with the previous lysate, then incubated overnight

at 4 °C.

Lysates were first clarified by spinning at 3,200g for 30 minutes and then added to

Beckman Quick-Seal tubes via 16 G 5” needles (Air-Tite N165). Iodixanol layers of increasing

density were then sequentially added as follows to form a gradient: 9 mL 15% iodixanol in 500

mM NaCl and 1× PBS-MK (1× PBS, 1 mM MgCl2 and 2.5 mM KCl), 6 mL 25% iodixanol in 1×

PBS-MK, and 5 mL each of 40% and 60% iodixanol in 1× PBS-MK. Phenol red at a final

concentration of 1 µg/mL was added to the 15, 25 and 60% layers to facilitate identification.

Ultracentrifugation was performed using a Ti 70 rotor in a Sorvall wX+ ultracentrifuge (Thermo

Fisher) at 68,000 rpm for 1 hour at 18 °C. Immediately following centrifugation, 3 mL of

solution was withdrawn from the 40–60% iodixanol interface via an 18 G needle. The solution

was exchanged at least 8000-fold into cold 1× PBS containing 0.001% F-68 using

polyethersulfone 100 kD MWCO columns (Thermo Fisher, Pierce 88533) and concentrated. The

concentrated AAV solution was sterile filtered using a 0.22 µm spin filter, quantified by qPCR

(AAVpro titration kit version 2; Clontech) and stored at 4 °C until use.

rAAV9 delivery

At P0, mice were sexed and genotyped, and homozygous Cln2R207X-/- mice were randomly

assigned to either PBS or ABE treatment groups. Following hypothermic sedation, P1 animals


<!-- Page 49 -->


38

received a single 5 µL intracerebroventricular (ICV) injection of either PBS, rAAV9.SpCas9–

ABE7.10 or rAAV9.SpCas9–ABE8eV106W at a total dose of 5.0 × 1010 vg/mouse (2.5 × 1010

vg/mouse/intein). Following injection, all animals were monitored until fully recovered. Mice

were monitored daily for the duration of the study by a trained animal technician.

Tissue collection

All animals were collected under an approved IACUC protocol. As previously described,

mice were sacrificed by CO2 inhalation at a flow rate of 3 L/min followed by diaphragm

puncture and subsequent cardiac perfusion with ice-cold saline146. Briefly, brains were removed,

sub-dissected, and collected for various assays. Additional peripheral tissues including heart,

liver, kidney, spleen, spinal cord, and eyes were collected into either 4% paraformaldehyde

(PFA) or flash frozen.

RNAscope imaging

Brains were carefully removed from euthanized mice, placed in a sagittal brain block,

and tissue blocks from 0–2 mm right of midline were flash frozen on dry ice. Flash frozen brains

were sectioned on a cryostat at 16 µm thickness with post-fixation in 10% formalin and serial

ethanol dehydration. Sections were then placed on slides and prepared for RNAscope labeling

per the manufacturer’s protocol (Advanced Cell Diagnostics, Newark, CA). Sections were

counterstained with DAPI and labeled with both N-intein and C-intein specific probes. Cover

slips were mounted onto labeled slides using antifade aqueous mounting media (Abcam,

ab104135) and imaged on a Nikon A1R Ti2E confocal and associated Nikon software.

RNAscope colocalization analysis

The total number of DAPI+ cells was quantified using CellProfiler software. Briefly, a 1

µm outline was applied to each DAPI+ nucleus, and a mask was overlaid to indicate individual

cells. Cells expressing both C-intein transcript and N-intein transcript were then quantified as a

percentage of total number of DAPI+ cells, representing the number of co-labeled cells out of

total cells. Analysis was performed in the motor cortex, visual cortex, somatosensory cortex,

thalamus, and hippocampus.

Immunohistochemistry

The left hemispheres of collected brains were fixed in 4% PFA for 48 hours, set in 3–5%

agarose, and vibratome sectioned into 96-well plates where they were sealed and stored at 4 °C

until immunohistochemistry analysis. Free-floating immunohistochemistry was performed as

previously described using anti-GFAP (Dako, Z0334), anti-ATP synthase subunit C (Abcam,

ab181243), and anti-CD68 (AbD Serotec, MCA1957) (124). Secondary antibodies included

biotinylated anti-rabbit (BA-1000; Vector Labs) and anti-rat (BA-9400; Vector Labs). Labeled

brain sections were placed on slides, allowed to dry overnight, and mounted using xylene and

xylene-based mounting media (Sigma Aldrich).

Imaging

Immunolabeled sections were imaged using an Aperio® AT2 microscope slide scanner

(Leica Biosystems, Wetzlar, Germany). Three images from brain regions of interest were taken

from each animal and signal intensities were quantified with ImageJ software.

### 3.1 Introduction

The ability to make targeted changes to the genome of living systems continues to

advance the life sciences and medicine. Double-strand break (DSB)-mediated DNA editing

strategies that use programmable nucleases, such as ZFNs, TALENs or CRISPR–Cas nucleases,

can efficiently disrupt genes by inducing insertions or deletions (indels) at the target site, but

DSBs also result in outcomes that are often undesired, including uncontrolled mixtures of editing

outcomes39,147, larger DNA rearrangements35,37,148, p53 activation36,149,150 and

chromothrypsis38,151. Although targeted DSBs can stimulate precise gene correction through

homology-directed repair, the process is inefficient in most therapeutically relevant cell types32.

In contrast, base editors40,47 and prime editors41 can efficiently install precise changes in

therapeutically relevant cells without requiring DSBs. Cytosine and adenosine base editors

enable the conversion of C•G to T•A and A•T to G•C, respectively, whereas prime editors enable

the installation of virtually any local mutation, including the substitution, insertion and/or

deletion of up to dozens of base pairs at targeted DNA sites.

Prime editing (PE) systems minimally consist of two components: a protein containing a

programmable DNA nickase fused to an engineered reverse transcriptase (RT) and a pegRNA

(Figure 3.1a)41. The pegRNA contains a spacer that specifies the target site, a single-guide RNA

(sgRNA) scaffold and a 3′ extension that encodes the desired edit. This extension contains a

primer binding site (PBS) that is complementary to a portion of the DNA protospacer and an RT

template that encodes the desired edit and downstream genomic sequence. After the PE

ribonucleoprotein (RNP) binds the target site and nicks the PAM-containing DNA strand, the

resulting nicked DNA strand base pairs to the PBS in the pegRNA, priming the reverse

transcription of the RT template directly into the target DNA site41. The newly synthesized 3′ flap

The versatility of PE arises from the ability of the 3′ extension of the pegRNA to encode

a wide variety of edited sequences. Despite its versatility, the efficiency of current prime editors

varies considerably among target sites and cell types41. Here we report that the putative

degradation of the 3′ extension of pegRNAs can erode PE efficiency. Although the resulting

truncated pegRNAs compete for target site engagement, they are incompetent for PE. To address

this vulnerability, we identified RNA motifs that protect pegRNA integrity and broadly improve

PE efficiencies at a variety of target sites in multiple cell lines and via multiple delivery

modalities. The resulting epegRNAs substantially advance the effectiveness and the application

scope of PE.

### 3.2 Results

3.2.1 RNA stability limits pegRNA efficacy

Unprotected nuclear RNAs are susceptible to degradation from both the 5′ and 3′ termini

by exonucleases152. In contrast to sgRNAs in which the entire guide RNA is protected by an

associated Cas9 protein153, the 3′ extension of pegRNAs is likely to be exposed in cells and, thus,

more susceptible to exonucleolytic degradation. We hypothesized that, although partially

degraded pegRNAs might retain their ability to bind Cas9 and engage the target DNA site, loss

or truncation of the PBS might prevent their ability to install the desired edit, thereby occupying

PE proteins and target sites with guide RNAs that cannot mediate PE.

To test this hypothesis, we transfected HEK293T cells with mixtures of two plasmids in

varying ratios that generate either (1) a full-length pegRNA containing an RT template encoding

a T•A-to-A•T transversion or (2) a truncated pegRNA containing an RT template encoding a


<!-- Page 57 -->


46

T•A-to-G•C transversion but lacking the PBS at the 3′ terminus. The two pegRNAs targeted

either the same or different genomic loci in human cells. We also tested the effect of adding a

plasmid that generated a non-interacting SaCas9 pegRNA that should compete for transcription

with the SpCas9 pegRNA-encoding plasmids but not interact with the prime editor protein.

Increasing the production of truncated pegRNA resulted in inhibited PE activity when the full-

length and truncated pegRNAs were targeted to the same site (Figure 3.1b). In contrast, neither a

truncated pegRNA targeted to a different genomic site nor a non-targeting SpCas9 sgRNA

impeded PE activity any more than the SaCas9 pegRNA (Figure 3.1b). These data suggest that

degraded pegRNAs with truncated 3′ extensions inhibit PE activity by enabling editing-

incompetent prime editor RNPs to compete for the targeted genomic locus.

3.2.2 Design of epegRNAs that improve PE efficiency

Having identified truncated pegRNAs as a potent inhibitor of PE, we next sought to

minimize pegRNA degradation. We envisioned that structured RNA motifs at the 3′ end of the

pegRNA (Figure 3.1c) might improve pegRNA stability, consistent with the ability of RNA

structures at the 5′ or 3′ termini to enhance mRNA stability in human cells and in yeast154,155. For

instance, the long-non-coding RNA MALAT1 is stabilized by a triple helix that sequesters its

poly(A) tail, limiting both degradation and nuclear export156.

We first tested whether PE efficiency could be improved by incorporating one of two

stable pseudoknots at the 3′ end of the pegRNA: either a modified prequeosine1-1 riboswitch

aptamer157,158 (evopreQ1) or the frameshifting pseudoknot from Moloney murine leukemia virus

(MMLV)159, hereafter referred to as ‘mpknot’. We chose evopreQ1 because it is one of the

smallest naturally derived RNA structural motifs with a defined tertiary structure (42 nucleotides

(nt) in length)157,158. We reasoned that smaller motifs would minimize the formation of secondary


<!-- Page 58 -->


47

structures that could interfere with pegRNA function. Furthermore, shorter pegRNAs can be

more easily produced by chemical synthesis. We chose mpknot because of its tertiary structure

and because it is an endogenous template for the MMLV RT from which the RT in canonical

prime editors was engineered, raising the possibility that mpknot might help recruit the RT. We

tested if these epegRNAs could insert a FLAG epitope tag sequence using PE3 at five genomic

loci in HEK293T cells (Figure 3.2a). To reduce the potential for the motif to interfere with

pegRNA function during PE, we included an 8-nt linker to connect either evopreQ1 or mpknot to

the 3′ end of the epegRNA PBS. Linker sequences were designed using ViennaRNA160 to avoid

potential base pairing interactions between the linker and PBS or between the linker and the

pegRNA spacer41. We observed an average of 2.1-fold increased efficiency of FLAG tag

insertion when using epegRNAs compared to canonical pegRNAs across all five genomic sites

tested, with no apparent change in edit:indel ratios, suggesting that 3′ terminal pseudoknot motifs

can improve PE efficacy.

We characterized the necessity of the linker sequence by comparing the ability of

epegRNAs with or without 8-nt linkers to mediate transversions or FLAG tag insertions. We

observed a significant decrease in PE3 editing efficiency upon removing the linker for

epegRNAs containing mpknot (P = 0.022) but no significant difference for epegRNAs that

contain evopreQ1 (Figure 3.3), perhaps because evopreQ1 is smaller than mpknot and is less

prone to steric clashes with the RT. Although the overall average editing efficiencies for

epegRNAs with evopreQ1 were similar (with or without a linker), we noted occasionally reduced

performance for epegRNAs without a linker (Figure 3.3). We therefore opted to include an 8-nt

linker, unless otherwise noted, for subsequent epegRNA designs.

3.2.4 Effect of epegRNAs on off-target PE

Previous studies showed that PE results in substantially less off-target editing than other

CRISPR gene editing strategies41,67,69,161,162. To determine if the addition of evopreQ1 or mpknot

changed the extent of off-target editing, we treated HEK293T cells with pegRNAs or epegRNAs

targeting HEK3, EMX1 or FANCF that template either a transversion (T•A-to-A•T at HEK3 or

G•C-to-T•A at EMX1 and FANCF) or a 15-bp deletion using PE3. We measured the extent of

indel generation and any nucleotide changes that could reasonably arise from PE at the top four

experimentally confirmed off-target sites163 for each targeted locus and compared the extent of

off-target editing between epegRNAs and unmodified pegRNAs after treatment with PE3. In all

cases, epegRNAs and pegRNAs exhibited ≤0.1% off-target PE and indels at the examined sites

(Figure 3.5), suggesting that epegRNAs and pegRNAs exhibit similar levels of off-target editing.

3.2.5 Basis of enhanced PE with epegRNAs

epegRNAs might enhance PE outcomes through a variety of mechanisms, including

resistance to degradation, higher expression levels, more efficient Cas9 binding and/or target

DNA engagement when complexed with Cas9; we probed each of these possibilities.

To determine whether evopreQ1 or mpknot impede degradation of the pegRNA 3′

extension, we compared the stability of epegRNAs and pegRNAs after in vitro incubation with

HEK293T nuclear lysates containing endogenous exonucleases. We found that pegRNAs were

degraded to a greater extent from this treatment compared to epegRNAs (1.9-fold compared to

evopreQ1 and 1.8-fold compared to mpknot, P < 0.005; Figure 3.6a). Conversely, the addition of

Cas9, which binds the guide RNA scaffold and is likely to protect the core sgRNA from

degradation, rescued pegRNA abundance compared to either epegRNA as determined by RT–

qPCR quantification of the guide RNA scaffold (Figure 3.6b).


<!-- Page 66 -->


55

The ability of 3′ structural motifs to increase the abundance of the upstream scaffold

region (Figure 3.6b) suggests that pegRNA degradation in the nucleus is dominated by 3′-

directed degradation. This model is consistent with the characterized behavior of the nuclear

exosome, which is the major source of RNA turnover in the nucleus164. However, partially

degraded pegRNAs would generate editing-incompetent RNPs previously shown to inhibit PE

(Figure 3.1c).

Next, to detect the activity of partially degraded RNAs in cells, we examined genomic PE

intermediates. In our current model, the 3′ flap intermediate generated by RT extension of the

nicked targeted site is converted into a 5′ flap intermediate, replacing the original genomic

sequence with the newly synthesized one41. This 5′ flap is then removed by 5′–3′ exonucleases,

and the resulting genomic nick undergoes ligation to install the prime edit41. Although full-length

pegRNAs would be expected to efficiently template RT extension of the nicked genomic strand,

truncated pegRNAs without a PBS should be unable to do so, resulting instead in nicking of the

targeted strand followed by chew-back or extension of the strand by DNA repair enzymes

(lacking the templated edit in either case). If a greater fraction of RT-extended PE intermediates

is observed with epegRNAs than with pegRNAs, this would suggest that addition of 3′ RNA

motifs improve the integrity of the PBS.

To capture these intermediates, we transfected HEK293T cells with plasmids encoding

PE2 and either unmodified pegRNAs or epegRNAs containing evopreQ1 or mpknot that template

transversions at HEK3, DNMT1, EMX1 or RNF2. Next, we used terminal transferase to label

with oligo-dG the 3′ termini of genomic DNA, which should include intermediates of PE that

have not yet undergone ligation. In each case, epegRNAs reduced the extent of editing-

incompetent intermediates at the targeted site by an average of 2.2-fold across the four sites

prime editors bound to truncated pegRNAs.

Because single-stranded 3′ termini are a common feature of 3′ exonuclease substrates165,

we next tested whether the degradation resistance conferred by these motifs could be explained

by the more mechanically stable tertiary structures of pseudoknots166. Notably, appending 15-bp

(34-nt) hairpins to the 3′ terminus resulted in inconsistent improvements to PE efficiency

compared to appending pseudoknots (Figure 3.6h), suggesting that tertiary structure is indeed an

important feature of epegRNAs.

To test if tertiary pseudoknot structure is required for epegRNA-mediated improvements

in PE efficiency, we examined the editing efficiency of epegRNAs containing the 15G>C point

mutation within evopreQ1, a mutation known to disrupt pseudoknot formation158. We used

epegRNAs to install a 24-bp FLAG epitope tag insertion, a 15-bp deletion or transversions

at HEK3 or RNF2 in HEK293T cells using PE3. Indeed, incorporation of the G15C mutation into

evopreQ1 abolished the increases in editing efficiency (Figure 3.6d). These results establish that

the secondary or tertiary structure of the motifs are critical for epegRNA-mediated PE

improvements, likely by stabilizing the 3′ extension.

3.2.7 A computational tool to design epegRNA linkers

In contrast with protein linkers, RNA linkers more likely to be sequence dependent, such

that the same linker might function for one epegRNA but impede another. To minimize the

possibility of interference from the epegRNA linker, we developed pegLIT (pegRNA Linker

Identification Tool) (Figure 3.12a), a computational tool that identifies linker sequences

predicted to minimally base pair with the remainder of the epegRNA. pegLIT uses simulated

annealing to sample the analyzed linker space efficiently175. Linkers that are adenosine- or

cytosine-rich are preferred by pegLIT since these nucleotides have been reported to function

better as flexible RNA linkers176. Additionally, pegLIT filters out linkers that contain runs of

four or more uridines, since such sequences could cause premature transcriptional termination177.

The pegLIT tool then analyzes linkers that pass these requirements using ViennaRNA160 to

predict potential interactions between the linker sequence and the pegRNA spacer, PBS,

template, or scaffold. The base pair probabilities of these predicted interactions are used to

generate subscores for each region of the pegRNA, each of which represents the degree to which

the linker is predicted to avoid interaction with the associated region. For example, a subscore of

0.95 for the PBS essentially indicates that, on average, the predicted probability of a pegRNA

folded state lacking base pairing between any linker nucleotide and the PBS is 95%.

We first sought to validate the use of pegLIT for linker design and to examine which

interactions identified by pegLIT were most detrimental to editing efficiency. We tested two

sets of 15 evopreQ1 epegRNAs with different linkers templating either a C•G-to-A•T

transversion at RNF2 or a 15-bp deletion at DNMT1. Within each set, five linkers were

recommended by pegLIT; five were predicted to base pair with the spacer; and five were

predicted to base pair with the PBS. The average spacer and PBS subscores were 0.94 and 0.97

for the optimal sequences, 0.66 and .95 for the spacer sequences, and 0.86 and 0.21 for the PBS

sequences. The use of pegLIT-designed linkers resulted in a modest increase in PE3 editing

efficiency over the use of manually designed linkers (1.2-fold higher for RNF2 and 1.1-fold

higher for DNMT1) (Figure 3.12b). Although spacer interactions did not significantly affect

editing efficiency, linker–PBS interactions correlated with reduced PE3 editing efficiency,

resulting in 1.3- and 1.1-fold lower editing efficiency compared to pegLIT linkers

for RNF2 and DNMT1, respectively. The two worst-performing linkers, which resulted in 1.9-

and 3.4-fold less efficient PE3 editing at RNF2 relative to optimal linker sequences, were

correctly identified by pegLIT as scoring poorly for PBS interactions (Figure 3.12c). The closer

proximity of the linker to the PBS compared to the spacer might give linker–PBS interactions an

entropic advantage compared to linker–spacer pairing. We then sought to determine whether

pegLIT-designed linker sequences could improve the efficacy of two epegRNAs (templating a

G•C-to-T•A transversion at EMX1 and a 15-bp deletion at VEGFA), which initially failed to

exhibit improved editing (Figure 3.4h,j). Indeed, using pegLIT-designed linkers increased PE3

editing efficiency by 1.3-fold and 1.4-fold, respectively, over that of pegRNAs for these two

edits (Figure 3.12d). Collectively, these findings demonstrate that pegLIT facilitates the use of

epegRNAs to consistently improve PE outcomes.

We also examined whether pegLIT-designed linkers improved the activity of epegRNAs

compared to epegRNAs without linkers. Compared to mpknot epegRNAs without a linker,

adding a pegLIT-designed linker resulted in a significantly increased editing efficiency than

when using manually designed linkers (Figure 3.3 and Figure 3.12f). In contrast, the use of

pegLIT linkers with evopreQ1 or tevopreQ1 epegRNAs did not significantly increase editing

relative to epegRNAs without a linker (Figure 3.12f,g). We therefore recommend the use of

pegLIT-designed linkers in epegRNAs using larger structured RNA motifs such as mpknot.

3.2.8 Improved editing efficiency with chemically modified epegRNAs

Chemically synthesized guide RNAs are commonly used when transfecting cells with

mRNA or RNPs178. Although synthetic guide RNAs can incorporate chemical modifications that

promote resistance to exonucleolytic degradation153,178, we speculated that structural motifs

might still mediate additional improvements in conjunction with such modifications.

To test this possibility, we compared PE efficiencies of synthetic tevopreQ1 epegRNAs

with those of synthetic pegRNAs that install either a point mutation or a 15-bp deletion at five

genomic sites (HEK3, RNF2, DNMT1, RUNX1 and EMX1) in HEK293T cells. Both the

epegRNAs and pegRNAs contained 2′-O-methyl modifications and phosphorothioate linkages

between the first and last three nucleotides of the RNA. For six of the seven pegRNAs tested, the

corresponding epegRNAs exhibited 1.1–3.1-fold higher editing with unchanged edit:indel ratios

(Figure 3.13). These data suggest that epegRNAs also enhance PE outcomes compared to

pegRNAs in applications that use chemically synthesized and modified pegRNAs.

### 3.3 Discussion

Here we report the design, characterization and validation of epegRNAs to address a key

bottleneck in PE. These epegRNAs contain a structured RNA motif 3′ of the PBS that prevents

degradation of the pegRNA extension and the subsequent formation of editing-incompetent PE

complexes that compete for access to the targeted genomic site. We found that epegRNAs

broadly improve PE efficiency in all five cell lines and primary cell types tested, with larger

improvements observed in cell lines that are more difficult to transfect. Additionally, we

observed that the use of epegRNAs can enhance PE performance when using chemically

modified pegRNAs, when installing therapeutically relevant edits in human cells and when using

unoptimized pegRNA designs. Finally, we describe a computational program that expedites

epegRNA design by identifying linkers that minimize the risk of counterproductive secondary

structure. In total, our findings establish that epegRNAs broadly improve PE outcomes at a wide

variety of genomic loci, edit types (substitutions, insertions and deletions) and cell types.

Improvements in PE enabled by epegRNAs are likely to depend on delivery strategy.

Lower-expression delivery modalities, such as some viral vectors, might benefit more strongly

from the use of epegRNAs when pegRNA concentration is limiting (Figure 3.11). Similarly,

further improvements in the synthesis of chemically modified RNAs might decrease the benefits

of epegRNAs by better mitigating degradation. Additionally, the longer length of epegRNAs (an

additional 37 nt when using tevopreQ1) is an important consideration when using synthetic

epegRNAs, given current challenges of chemically synthesizing longer RNAs.


<!-- Page 89 -->


78

We recommend epegRNAs for all PE experiments that can support a modestly longer

pegRNA. Importantly, researchers seeking to identify PE agents that install a desired edit with

the highest possible efficiency should continue to test many epegRNAs that include a variety of

PBS and RT template sequences and lengths and a variety of nicking sgRNAs when using PE3.

As demonstrated in this study, however, extensive screening might not be needed when

maximizing editing efficiency is not critical. In these cases, an epegRNA containing the trimmed

evopreQ1 (tevopreQ1) motif with a PBS length of 13 and a template that includes either 10 nt of

homology past the targeted edit for small insertions, deletions and point mutations—or 25 nt of

homology for larger insertions or deletions—provides a promising starting point for epegRNA

designs. PBS, RT template length, scaffold sequence and nicking sgRNA can then be optimized

if observed editing efficiencies are insufficient.

### 3.4 Methods

General methods

Plasmids expressing pegRNAs and epegRNAs were cloned by Gibson assembly, Golden

Gate assembly using either a previously described custom acceptor plasmid41 or newly designed

custom acceptor plasmids that contain trimmed evopreQ1 or mpknot or synthesized and cloned

by Twist Biosciences. Plasmids expressing sgRNAs were cloned via Gibson or USER assembly.

DNA amplification was accomplished by PCR with Phusion U or High Fidelity Phusion Green

Hot Start II (New England Biolabs). Plasmids expressing pegRNAs were purified using

PureYield Plasmid Miniprep kits (Promega) when transfecting HEK293T cells or Plasmid Plus

Midiprep kits (Qiagen) when transfecting other cell types, whereas plasmids expressing prime

editors were purified exclusively using Plasmid Plus Midiprep kits. Plasmids ordered from Twist


<!-- Page 90 -->


79

Biosciences were resuspended in nuclease-free water and used directly. Primers and dsDNA

fragments were ordered from Integrated DNA Technologies.

Synthetics pegRNAs and in vitro transcribed mRNA generation

Synthetic pegRNAs were ordered from Integrated DNA Technologies and contained 2′-

O-methyl modifications at the first and last three nucleotides and phosphorothioate linkages

between the three first and last nucleotides and were used directly. Synthetic nicking sgRNAs

were ordered from Synthego and contained 2′-O-methyl modifications at the three first and last

nucleotides and phosphorothioate linkages between the first three and last two nucleotides. PE-

encoded mRNA was transcribed in vitro using the protocol described previously191. Briefly, the

PE2 cassette—consisting of a 5′ untranslated region (UTR), Kozak sequence, PE2 ORF and 3′

UTR—was cloned into a plasmid containing an inactive T7 (dT7) promoter. The mRNA

transcription template was generated via PCR using a primer to install the correct T7 promoter

sequence and a reverse primer that installed the poly(A) tail. mRNA was generated using a

HiScribe T7 High-Yield RNA Kit (New England Biolabs) according to the manufacturer’s

instructions, with the exception that N1-methylpseudouridine triphosphate (TriLink) was

substituted for uridine triphosphate, and CleanCapAG (TriLink) was added to enable co-

transcriptional capping. The resulting mRNA was purified via lithium chloride precipitation and

reconstituted in TE buffer (10 mM Tris, 1 mM EDTA, pH 8.0 at 25 °C). Sequences of pegRNAs

and sgRNAs as well as a list of structured RNA motifs used in this study can be found in the

supplementary materials of the article this chapter is adapted from.

High-throughput DNA sequencing of genomic DNA samples

Genomic sites of interest were amplified from genomic DNA samples and sequenced on

an Illumina MiSeq as previously described41. Cas9 off-target sites for HEK3, EMX1 and FANCF

were previously identified via Guide-Seq163. Primers used for mammalian cell genomic DNA

amplification and related amplicon sequences can be found in the supplementary materials of the

article this chapter is adapted from. Sequencing reads were demultiplexed using MiSeq Reporter

(Illumina). Alignment of amplicon sequences to a reference sequence was performed using

CRISPResso2 (ref. 145). For all PE yield quantifications, editing efficiency was calculated as the

percentage of reads with the desired editing without indels out of the total number of reads with

an average phred score of at least 30. For quantification of point mutation editing, CRISPResso2

was run in standard mode with ‘discard_indel_reads’ on. Editing yield was calculated as the

percentage of non-discarded reads containing the edit divided by total reads. For insertion or

deletion edits, CRISPResso2 was run in homology-directed repair mode using the desired allele

as the expected allele and with ‘discard_indel_reads’ on. Editing yield was calculated as the

percentage of homology-directed repair aligned reads divided by total reads. For all experiments,

indel frequency was calculated as the number of discarded reads divided by the total number of

reads. For experiments involving PE2, reads were analyzed for indels within 10 nt upstream and

downstream of the pegRNA nick site, inclusive. For experiments involving PE3, reads were

analyzed for indels between 10 nt upstream of the pegRNA nick site and downstream from the

sgRNA nick site, inclusive. Off-target editing was quantified as described previously41.

Linker design via pegLIT

To design epegRNA linker sequences, we wrote a custom algorithm, called the pegRNA

Linker Identification Tool, or pegLIT, that searches for linker sequences of a specified length that

minimize base pairing with the remainder of the pegRNA. To reduce computing time, this

procedure uses simulated annealing to maximize subscores175, each of which corresponds to a

subsequence of the pegRNA: PBS, spacer, template and then scaffold. Accordingly, different

linker sequences might be generated for the same epegRNA if the algorithm is run multiple

times. During optimization, the higher-scoring linker in any pair of linkers was determined by

comparing their discretized subscores in order of the following subsequence priority: spacer,

PBS, template and then scaffold. Each subscore is calculated, using base pair probabilities

calculated by ViennaRNA 2.0 (ref. 160) under standard parameters (37 °C, 1 M NaCl, 0.05 M

MgCl2), as the complement of the mean probability that a nucleotide in the linker forms a base

pair with any nucleotide in the pegRNA subsequence under consideration, where the mean is

taken over all bases in the linker. Linker sequences with AC content <50% and those that would

result in a pegRNA containing four of the same nucleotide consecutively are removed from

consideration174,176. Optionally, the algorithm performs hierarchical agglomerative clustering on

the 100 highest-scoring linkers and outputs one linker per cluster to promote sequence diversity

in the final output. Our Python implementation of pegLIT is publicly accessible

at peglit.liugroup.us, and the code can be found below or at github.com/sshen8/peglit.

### 4.1 Introduction

Modern advances in oncology have been greatly advanced by improvements in our

ability to distinguish between cancer cells and healthy cells on a genetically encodable basis.

Improvements in high-throughput sequencing technologies that make routine large-scale

sequencing of genomes and transcriptomes feasible, culminating in resources such as The Cancer

Genome Atlas194, have enabled the discovery of genetic vulnerabilities for many cancers such as

BRAF V600E in melanoma195 and activating EGFR mutations in non-small cell lung cancer196.

The resulting targeted therapies that exploit these biomarkers, including vemurafenib197 and

gefitinib198 respectively for the aforementioned examples, have become foundational

components of cancer treatment in the relevant patient cohorts. However, the emergence of drug

resistance within the tumor population, leading to relapse, is a common problem for targeted

therapies directed against a single oncoprotein199-201.

Immunotherapies, particularly immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs), have been able to

produce astonishingly durable tumor responses in patients101,202. These drugs block

immunoinhibitory interactions such as that between programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1) and

programmed cell death ligand 1 (PD-L1), resulting in broadly improved T cell responses that

mediate tumor clearance100. While all arms of the adaptive immune system are involved in the

body’s response to cancer, CD8+ T cells are a central pillar, being able to directly recognize and

kill cancer cells based on the display of neoepitopes on major histocompatibility complex class I

(MHC-I) proteins expressed on the surface of all nucleated cells103. This mechanism allows

CD8+ T cells to exploit any of the thousands of coding mutations found in cancer genomes in

principle102, which likely contributes to the durable therapeutic response ICIs can achieve.


<!-- Page 111 -->


100

In practice, adaptions that reduce susceptibility to CD8+ T cell attack such as

downregulation of MHC-I or loss of β2-microglobulin have been described in patient tumors203.

However, the mutation burden of a tumor is correlated with likelihood of response to ICI

therapy102, suggesting that simply having fewer targetable neoepitopes is also a strategy utilized

by certain cancers to escape the immune system. This is made feasible by the strict requirements

for successful presentation on MHC-I; somatic mutations must occur proximal to an anchor

residue and produce an amino acid change significant enough to be recognized as foreign104.

From thousands of coding mutations, only a handful will provoke significant immune responses

to none at all in the case of immunologically cold tumors118.

Extending the benefits of ICI therapy to these low mutation burden cancers is

mechanistically challenging given the lack of immune recognition to augment. Here we describe

the potential of prime editing to address this challenge via the installation of immunogenic

epitope sequences to produce a de novo immune response. Prime editing is a novel genome

editing technology that can programmably generate all single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs)

as well as insertions or deletions up to hundreds of base pairs in size41,62. It functions by using a

Cas9 nickase, fused to a reverse transcriptase, to expose a DNA primer that can hybridize with

the 3′ extension of a prime editing guide RNA (pegRNA). The reverse transcriptase then extends

the DNA using the pegRNA 3′ extension as a template, copying over the desired edit in the

process. We demonstrate that prime editing can be used to sensitize tumor cells to T cell attack,

and that partial epitope expression improves response to an anti-cancer vaccine modeled with

ovalbumin (OVA). Finally, we show that in vivo prime editing improves response to vaccine and

ICI combination therapy in the B16-F10 melanoma model.
